# Exercise 1.1 — Python vs R {#sec-python-r}

:::: {.web-only}
Every cell on this page is a real R or Python cell. Copy the code in your chosen
language, run it, and read the output. Then read the other tab. The point is not
to memorise either one — it is to be able to open a colleague's script in the
language you do not use and still follow what it does.
::::

## Why both

The two languages carry two different ideas of what an analysis *is*. In R the
thing you hold is the data frame, and the verbs act on whole columns. In Python
the thing you hold is an object, and you call methods on it. Most of what looks
unfamiliar in the other language comes from that one difference, so it is worth
keeping in mind as you read.

This page walks through the four libraries you will use most, one pairing at a
time: the Python library first by name, then the R package that does the same
job.

## The data

Five patients, two columns: `age` in years, and `score`, an Injury Severity
Score. Small enough that you can check every result by eye, which is the only
reason to use a toy dataset — from @sec-pipeline onwards the files are real
extracts with real problems.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
data <- data.frame(
  age   = c(23, 45, 12, 56, 70),
  score = c(87, 56, 30, 77, 80)
)
data
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd

data = pd.DataFrame({
    "age":   [23, 45, 12, 56, 70],
    "score": [87, 56, 30, 77, 80]
})
data
```
:::

## `pandas` → `dplyr`, from the tidyverse

Both are for data wrangling: selecting, filtering, sorting, summarising. Here,
keeping only the patients over 20.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

filtered_data <- data %>% filter(age > 20)
head(filtered_data)
```

## Python

```{python}
filtered_data = data[data["age"] > 20]
filtered_data.head()
```
:::

Read the two side by side. `filter(age > 20)` names the column directly, because
dplyr already knows which frame you mean. `data[data["age"] > 20]` has to name
the frame twice: once to build the vector of `True`/`False`, once to subset with
it. Same result, different notion of where the data lives.

## `scikit-learn` → `tidymodels`

Both are for building machine learning pipelines. Here, fitting a linear
regression of score on age.

In R you have already done this in Module 2, with `lm()` from the `stats`
package in base R:

```{r}
model <- lm(score ~ age, data = data)
summary(model)
```

In Python the same fit comes from scikit-learn:

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model_py = LinearRegression()
X = data[["age"]]    # 2-D: a frame, because sklearn expects a matrix of predictors
y = data["score"]    # 1-D: a series, the target

model_py.fit(X, y)
print(model_py.intercept_, model_py.coef_)
```

The coefficients agree. They are a property of the data, not of the software,
and that is the reassuring half of this page.

What differs is what each returns. `lm()` hands back a statistical summary —
standard errors, residuals, an F test — because R's linear model was written for
inference. `LinearRegression` hands back coefficients and a `.predict()` method,
because scikit-learn's was written for prediction. Neither is wrong; they were
built to answer different questions.

R can also do it the scikit-learn way. `tidymodels` sets the model up in the
same three moves — define the algorithm, give it the data, fit it:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidymodels)

lm_model <- linear_reg() %>%
            set_engine("lm") %>%      # use lm()'s implementation underneath
            set_mode("regression")

lm_fit <- lm_model %>%
          fit(score ~ age, data = data)

lm_fit[["fit"]][["coefficients"]]
```

Note what `set_engine("lm")` is doing: the specification above says *linear
regression* and nothing about how to compute it, and the engine supplies the
arithmetic. Swap in `"glmnet"` and the first half of that code is unchanged.
That separation is what makes the pipeline in @sec-pipeline swappable, and it is
why `tidymodels` is worth the extra typing for a model `lm()` could have fitted
in one line.

## `seaborn` → `ggplot2`

Both are for plotting. Here, a scatter of score against age.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = score)) +
  geom_point()
```

## Python

```{python}
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.scatterplot(x = data["age"], y = data["score"])
plt.show()
```
:::

The `+` in ggplot2 is not decoration. A plot is a stack of layers and you add
them one at a time, which is why the next task is a one-line change rather than
a rewrite.

## `numpy` → base R

numpy is Python's array library; in R, arrays and the arithmetic on them are in
the language itself, so there is nothing to load. Here, a dot product.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
a <- c(1, 2, 3)
b <- c(4, 5, 6)
dot_product <- sum(a * b)
dot_product
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
dot_product = np.dot(a, b)
print(dot_product)
```
:::

`a * b` multiplies element by element in both languages, and `sum()` adds the
result. `np.dot` does both in one step. This is the pairing where R needs no
library at all, which is worth knowing when you read R code and cannot find the
import.

## Task — Put the regression on the plot

Add the fitted line to the scatter. In ggplot2 it is one more layer: look up
`geom_smooth()` and give it `method = "lm"`. Then find the Python equivalent —
seaborn has a function that draws a scatter *and* its regression line together.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = score)) +
  geom_point() +
  ______(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
#| message: false
ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = score)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

`se = FALSE` turns off the confidence band. Leave it on and you will see how
wide it is with five points, which is an honest picture of what this data can
support.
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
sns.______(x = "age", y = "score", data = data)
plt.show()
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
sns.regplot(x = "age", y = "score", data = data)
plt.show()
```

`sns.regplot()` draws the points and fits the line in one call. `sns.lmplot()`
does the same and will also split the plot by a grouping column.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
In R the layer you want starts with `geom_`. In Python the seaborn function you
want starts with `reg`.
:::

## Where to look things up

Take your time now and explore these two libraries a little further. When
something in class is unclear, these are the first places to look — both are
written to teach, not only to document:

- [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) — the user guide explains the
  statistics as well as the code
- [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org) — start with *Get Started*

A longer side-by-side comparison of the two languages, if you want one:
[occasionaldivergences.com/posts/python-intro](https://occasionaldivergences.com/posts/python-intro/).

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can filter, fit and plot in both languages, and that the
coefficients you obtained are a property of the data rather than of the software
that computed them.

**Cannot:** anything about how well this model predicts. Five patients, and every
number computed on the same five. That is where @sec-pipeline starts.
